name: Ruxolitinib cream
lead: Ruxolitinib cream (brand name Opzelura) is a prescription topical Janus kinase (JAK1/JAK2) inhibitor. The US FDA approved it in September 2021 for mild to moderate atopic dermatitis, described as the first topical JAK inhibitor approved in the US, and in July 2022 for nonsegmental vitiligo.[1][3]

Its appearance relevance is repigmentation. Vitiligo is an autoimmune condition in which pigment cells are lost, leaving pale patches that many people find visible, especially on the face and hands. In phase 3 trials, people who applied the cream regained pigment in facial and body patches, and the 1.5% cream is described as the first treatment approved in several countries for repigmentation in patients aged 12 and over.[2][3] Eczema control with the same product can also reduce visible redness and scaling on the face.[4]

The evidence base consists of vehicle-controlled phase 2 and phase 3 randomized trials in vitiligo and atopic dermatitis, with long-term extensions and a growing set of registered studies in other skin conditions.[2][5][6][7]
infobox: Prescription-only; boxed warning in the US[3]

paras: For appearance, the draw of ruxolitinib cream is repigmentation. Vitiligo leaves depigmented patches that are especially noticeable on darker skin and on exposed areas such as the face and hands, and the phase 3 program put facial repigmentation first: its primary endpoint was a 75% improvement in the facial Vitiligo Area Scoring Index, with the Vitiligo Noticeability Scale among the key secondary measures.[2][3]

Dermatology reviews describe the cream as changing the treatment landscape because it is the first approved option aimed at restoring pigment, rather than only halting spread.[8][9] Reviews of vitiligo management discuss oral JAK inhibitors as additional directions.[8][22] In atopic dermatitis, the cream's effect on visible redness, scaling and itch on the face and body is part of its appeal.[5][20]

Ruxolitinib cream is approved for nonsegmental vitiligo, the most common form, in people aged 12 and over. Dermatology reviews describe it as the first approved repigmentation treatment, in a field where earlier options such as topical corticosteroids and calcineurin inhibitors had limited efficacy.[3][8][9] Because vitiligo is limited to the skin, topical rather than systemic therapy is preferred where lesions are localised.[9]

The cream is also approved for mild to moderate atopic dermatitis, and a phase 3 study has examined children aged 2 to 11.[1][10] Trials have also been run in alopecia areata, prurigo nodularis, lichen planus, lichen sclerosus, genital vitiligo and hidradenitis suppurativa.[11][12][13][14][15][16]

Ruxolitinib inhibits JAK1 and JAK2, blocking JAK-STAT signaling that carries cytokine messages driving autoimmune and inflammatory skin disease. In vitiligo, interferon-gamma signaling through JAK1 and JAK2 is thought to direct immune cells against melanocytes, which is the rationale for the treatment.[1][3] Pharmacokinetic analyses of phase 2 and 3 atopic dermatitis trials and a maximum-use trial examined how much drug reaches the bloodstream after topical use.[6][17]

The topical route is intended to keep drug levels in the bloodstream low compared with the oral form, and pharmacokinetic studies including a maximum-use trial in adolescents and adults with atopic dermatitis measured the systemic exposure that results.[6][17] In vitiligo, repigmentation is described as slow: the phase 3 endpoint was measured at 24 weeks, with continued improvement reported through 52 weeks and beyond.[2][3]

In the vitiligo trials, the most common treatment-related adverse events were application-site acne, itching and exfoliation.[3] As with oral JAK inhibitors, the US label carries boxed warnings for serious infections, mortality, malignancy, major adverse cardiovascular events and thrombosis, although incidences were low with topical application in trials.[3] Long-term safety data in atopic dermatitis have been published from two phase 3 studies.[7]

Because topical ruxolitinib is a JAK inhibitor, the US label carries the same class boxed warnings as oral products, and the phase 3 vitiligo analyses report that serious events were uncommon over the study periods.[3] Application-site acne and itching were the most commonly reported reactions in vitiligo, and reviews note that treated areas on the face were among those studied for tolerability.[2][3]

Oral ruxolitinib was developed for blood disorders and is a long-established JAK inhibitor.[1] A topical formulation was developed by Incyte for skin disease. A phase 2 randomized trial in vitiligo was published in The Lancet in 2020, atopic dermatitis phase 3 results in 2021, and the vitiligo phase 3 trials in 2022.[18][19][2] The FDA approved the cream for atopic dermatitis in September 2021 and for vitiligo in July 2022.[1]

Oral ruxolitinib was developed by Incyte, marketed as Jakafi in the US and as Jakavi by Novartis elsewhere, and was approved in the US in November 2011 for myelofibrosis, with later approvals in polycythemia vera (2014) and graft-versus-host disease (2019 and 2021).[1] The cream, sold as Opzelura, was the first topical JAK inhibitor approved in the US, in September 2021 for atopic dermatitis, and gained its vitiligo indication in July 2022.[1] Wikipedia reports that the European Medicines Agency's committee gave a positive opinion for non-segmental vitiligo in February 2023.[1]

A phase 2 randomized dose-ranging trial in adults with vitiligo reported efficacy and safety over 52 weeks of double-blind treatment, the first controlled data for the cream in repigmentation.[18] The phase 3 program, TRuE-V1 and TRuE-V2, enrolled 674 patients aged 12 and over with nonsegmental vitiligo covering up to 10% of body surface area in North America and Europe. Patients were randomized 2:1 to 1.5% ruxolitinib cream or vehicle applied twice daily for 24 weeks, and then all could use the cream through week 52. The primary endpoint was at least 75% improvement in the facial Vitiligo Area Scoring Index (F-VASI75) at week 24, and key secondary endpoints included the Vitiligo Noticeability Scale; significantly more cream recipients met the endpoints than vehicle recipients, and efficacy continued to week 104 in longer-term analyses.[2][3]

In atopic dermatitis, two phase 3 trials evaluated 8-week efficacy and safety, a phase 2 study compared the cream with triamcinolone cream, a phase 2 analysis reported effects on itch and quality of life, and long-term phase 3 safety data are published.[19][20][21][7] A phase 3 trial in children aged 2 to 11 has also reported.[10] Phase 2 work in alopecia areata is published, and registered studies cover genital vitiligo, prurigo nodularis, lichen planus, lichen sclerosus and hidradenitis suppurativa.[11][12][13][14][15][16]

Opzelura is prescription-only. Wikipedia lists ruxolitinib as prescription-only in the US, Canada, the EU, the UK and Australia, and as an orphan drug for some oral indications.[1] Because it is a branded specialty product, access varies by country and insurance coverage, and vitiligo patient communities discuss it as the first approved repigmentation treatment while describing patience being needed for results.[3][9]

Reviews of vitiligo therapy discuss oral JAK inhibitors, including ruxolitinib and others, as further options being examined, and describe the topical cream as having changed the treatment landscape.[8][22]

card.summary: A prescription JAK-inhibitor cream approved for vitiligo repigmentation and eczema, backed by phase 3 trials.
card.note: Prescription-only; oral JAK inhibitors carry serious-infection warnings.

quick.overview:
Ruxolitinib cream (Opzelura) is a topical JAK inhibitor approved in the US for atopic dermatitis (2021) and vitiligo (2022).

For vitiligo it has phase 2 and two phase 3 randomized trials behind it, making it one of the better-studied treatments for skin repigmentation.
quick.mechanism: It inhibits JAK1 and JAK2 enzymes, damping the immune signaling involved in vitiligo and eczema.
quick.risks: Prescription only. Specific adverse events are listed in trial reports and the label; oral JAK inhibitors carry warnings on infections and blood counts.

chain: Dampens the immune attack on pigment cells
More even skin tone, especially on the face
angle.text: For people with nonsegmental vitiligo, the cream is applied to depigmented patches and in trials produced repigmentation of facial and body areas and lower patch noticeability. It is a prescription product used under dermatologist supervision.
